```{r}
#| label: setup-c
#| output: false
# SETUP FOR RENDERING THIS FILE ON ITS OWN.
# At the group merge, delete this chunk: phones_clean, phone_training and
# phone_prep come from Person B's chunks (same code, same seed).
library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse, tidymodels, here, gt)
tidymodels_prefer()

phones <- here("data/smartphone_cleaned_v5.csv") |>
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE)

phones_clean <- phones |>
  filter(!model %in% c("Vertu Signature Touch",
                       "Xiaomi Redmi K20 Pro Signature Edition")) |>
  mutate(
    log_price = log(price),
    has_5g = factor(if_else(as.logical(has_5g), "Yes", "No"),
                    levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    has_nfc = factor(if_else(as.logical(has_nfc), "Yes", "No"),
                     levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    brand_group = fct_relevel(fct_lump_n(brand_name, n = 7), "xiaomi")
  ) |>
  select(log_price, processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory,
         refresh_rate, primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front,
         battery_capacity, screen_size, has_5g, has_nfc, brand_group) |>
  na.omit()

set.seed(41352)
phone_split <- initial_split(phones_clean, prop = 0.75, strata = log_price)
phone_training <- training(phone_split)
phone_test <- testing(phone_split)

phone_rec <- recipe(log_price ~ ., data = phone_training) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_pca(processor_speed, ram_capacity, internal_memory, refresh_rate,
           primary_camera_rear, primary_camera_front,
           threshold = 0.7, id = "pca") |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

phone_prep <- prep(phone_rec)
```

```{r}
#| label: c-objects
#| output: false
# Person C objects. Uses phone_prep and phone_training from Person B.

# 1. Loadings: one row per specification x component (Week 7/8 PCA lecture)
pca_loadings <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "coef")

# Number of components kept by threshold = 0.7 (= PC columns after bake)
c_pc_scores <- bake(phone_prep, new_data = NULL) |>
  select(starts_with("PC"))
kept_pcs <- names(c_pc_scores)

# Variance explained by the kept components (for the text)
c_var <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "variance")
pc_pct <- c_var |>
  filter(terms == "percent variance", component <= length(kept_pcs)) |>
  pull(value)
pc_cum <- c_var |>
  filter(terms == "cumulative percent variance",
         component == length(kept_pcs)) |>
  pull(value)

# Readable names for the six specifications (units in brackets)
spec_vars <- c("processor_speed", "ram_capacity", "internal_memory",
               "refresh_rate", "primary_camera_rear", "primary_camera_front")
spec_labels <- c(
  processor_speed      = "Processor speed (GHz)",
  ram_capacity         = "RAM (GB)",
  internal_memory      = "Storage (GB)",
  refresh_rate         = "Refresh rate (Hz)",
  primary_camera_rear  = "Rear camera (MP)",
  primary_camera_front = "Front camera (MP)"
)

# Group style for charts: same colours and fonts as styles.css
theme_slides <- function(base_size = 16) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(text = element_text(colour = "#1F2933"),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = "#5F6B7A"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#E6ECF2"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1F4E79",
                                    size = rel(1.05), hjust = 0),
          legend.position = "top",
          legend.justification = "left")
}

# Group style for gt tables: navy header, light banding, no heavy borders
slide_table <- function(tbl, font_px = 18) {
  tbl |>
    opt_row_striping() |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = px(font_px),
                table.font.names = c("Source Sans 3", "Source Sans Pro",
                                     "Helvetica", "Arial", "sans-serif"),
                column_labels.background.color = "#1F4E79",
                column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
                row.striping.background_color = "#F4F7FA",
                table.border.top.color = "#1F4E79",
                table.border.bottom.color = "#D9E2EC",
                column_labels.border.bottom.color = "#1F4E79",
                table_body.hlines.color = "#E6ECF2",
                data_row.padding = px(6))
}

# Loading of one specification on one component (used in the text)
ld <- function(pc, spec) {
  pca_loadings |>
    filter(component == pc, terms == spec) |>
    pull(value) |>
    round(2)
}

# Sign check: signs can flip between computers (Week 7/8 lecture).
# Both must be TRUE for the component names below to be correct.
pc1_loadings <- pca_loadings |>
  filter(component == "PC1") |>
  pull(value)
pc1_all_positive <- all(pc1_loadings > 0)
pc2_storage_vs_camera <- ld("PC2", "internal_memory") > 0 &
  ld("PC2", "primary_camera_rear") < 0

# 2. Part (a) descriptive analysis: average specifications of phones with
#    low, middle and high component scores. bake() replaces the six specs
#    with PC1 and PC2, so join the scores back to the original training rows.
pc_profile <- bind_cols(phone_training, c_pc_scores)

profile_long <- map_dfr(kept_pcs, \(pc) {
  pc_profile |>
    mutate(group = ntile(.data[[pc]], 3),
           group = factor(group, levels = 1:3,
                          labels = c("Low", "Middle", "High"))) |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(phones = n(), across(all_of(spec_vars), mean)) |>
    pivot_longer(-group, names_to = "spec", values_to = "mean") |>
    mutate(component = pc)
})

# Average of one specification in one group (used in the text)
avg <- function(pc, grp, spec, digits = 0) {
  profile_long |>
    filter(component == pc, group == grp, spec == !!spec) |>
    pull(mean) |>
    round(digits)
}

# 3. Price map data: the training phones with their names, prices and
#    which side of PC2 they fall on. Rows of phone_training are
#    phones_clean[phone_split$in_id, ], so the model names line up exactly.
phones_named <- phones |>
  filter(!model %in% c("Vertu Signature Touch",
                       "Xiaomi Redmi K20 Pro Signature Edition")) |>
  select(model, price, all_of(spec_vars), battery_capacity, screen_size,
         has_5g, has_nfc, brand_name) |>
  na.omit()
# Safety check: same phones in the same order as phones_clean
stopifnot(nrow(phones_named) == nrow(phones_clean),
          all(phones_named[spec_vars] == phones_clean[spec_vars]))

# Currency: the dataset records prices in Indian rupees (INR). For a
# Malaysian audience the chart shows ringgit (MYR). Rate = midpoint of Bank
# Negara Malaysia's buying (4.2354) and selling (4.2393) rates for 100 INR,
# 6 October 2026, 5pm. Converting multiplies every price by the same number,
# so the PCA and every regression coefficient except the intercept are
# unchanged; only the chart's price axis changes.
myr_per_100_inr <- 4.2374
inr_to_myr <- myr_per_100_inr / 100

phone_map <- pc_profile |>
  mutate(model = phones_named$model[phone_split$in_id],
         price = exp(log_price) * inr_to_myr,
         focus = if_else(PC2 > 0, "Memory and speed focused", "Camera focused"),
         focus = factor(focus, levels = c("Memory and speed focused",
                                          "Camera focused")))

# Five well-known phones to label, with label offsets so they do not overlap
example_phones <- tribble(
  ~model,                        ~label,             ~nudge_x, ~nudge_y,
  "Redmi 12C",                   "Redmi 12C",         0.3,     -0.45,
  "Nothing Phone 1",             "Nothing Phone 1",   0.0,     -0.55,
  "OnePlus 11 5G",               "OnePlus 11",       -0.2,      0.40,
  "Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra 5G", "Galaxy S23 Ultra",  0.2,      0.38,
  "Apple iPhone 13",             "iPhone 13",        -0.9,      0.30
) |>
  inner_join(phone_map |> select(model, PC1, price, focus), by = "model")

focus_colours <- c("Memory and speed focused" = "#2C7FB8",
                   "Camera focused" = "#D95F02")

# Correlation between PC1 and log price (used in the text)
pc1_price_cor <- round(cor(phone_map$PC1, phone_map$log_price), 2)

# Price in ringgit of one labelled phone, rounded to RM 10 (used in the text)
ex_price <- function(phone) {
  example_phones |>
    filter(label == phone) |>
    pull(price) |>
    round(-1) |>
    scales::comma()
}

# One "low vs high" row for the part (a) slide: label | low | high
stat_row <- function(pc, spec, label, unit, digits = 0, down = FALSE) {
  lo <- avg(pc, "Low", spec, digits)
  hi <- avg(pc, "High", spec, digits)
  cls <- if (down) "stat down" else "stat"
  paste0('<div class="', cls, '"><span class="stat-label">', label,
         '</span><span class="stat-low">', lo, " ", unit,
         '</span><span class="stat-value">', hi, " ", unit, "</span></div>")
}

# Wide table for a slide: rows = specifications, columns = Low / Middle / High
profile_table <- function(pc) {
  profile_long |>
    filter(component == pc) |>
    select(-component) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = mean) |>
    mutate(spec = if_else(spec == "phones", "Phones",
                          unname(spec_labels[spec]))) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(spec = "Specification (average)") |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Low, Middle, High), decimals = 1) |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Low, Middle, High),
               rows = spec == "Processor speed (GHz)", decimals = 2) |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Low, Middle, High),
               rows = spec == "Phones", decimals = 0) |>
    slide_table()
}
```

# What do the components mean? {.center background-color="#1F4E79"}

Part (a): describing PC1 and PC2 with the six specifications

## Extracting the loadings {.smaller}

A **loading** (from −1 to 1) shows how strongly a specification moves with a component. This code produces @tbl-loadings on the next slide.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loadings
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|2-5|6-9"
#| tbl-cap: "Loadings of the six specifications on each retained component."
pca_loadings <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "coef")
pca_loadings |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  mutate(terms = spec_labels[terms]) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = terms, names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(terms = "Specification") |>
  fmt_number(columns = -terms, decimals = 2) |>
  slide_table(font_px = 26)
```

::: notes
Line 1 extracts the loadings from B's prepped recipe with tidy(type = "coef"); "pca" is the id B gave to step_pca. Lines 2 to 5 keep the components retained by the 70% threshold and put one column per component. Lines 6 to 9 format the table; slide_table() applies the group's table style. On the next slide: every PC1 loading is positive, while PC2 has positive and negative loadings.
:::

## Two components describe the hardware {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-top-loadings
#| fig-cap: "The three largest loadings on each component. Blue = positive, orange = negative."
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.4
pca_loadings |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  group_by(component) |>
  slice_max(abs(value), n = 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(spec = fct_reorder(unname(spec_labels[terms]), abs(value)),
         sign = if_else(value > 0, "Positive", "Negative")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = abs(value), y = spec, fill = sign)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ component, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Positive = "#2C7FB8", Negative = "#D95F02")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.8), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Absolute loading", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_slides()
```
:::

::::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .fragment}
[PC1 · `r round(pc_pct[1], 1)`% of the variance]{.kicker} [Overall performance]{.big}

- All six loadings are **positive** (`r round(min(pc1_loadings), 2)` to `r round(max(pc1_loadings), 2)`), led by RAM (@tbl-loadings)
- A phone strong in one specification is strong in all of them (@fig-top-loadings)
:::

::: {.card .orange .fragment}
[PC2 · `r round(pc_pct[2], 1)`% of the variance]{.kicker} [Storage and speed vs camera]{.big}

- Storage (`r ld("PC2", "internal_memory")`) is **positive**; rear (`r ld("PC2", "primary_camera_rear")`) and front cameras (`r ld("PC2", "primary_camera_front")`) are **negative** (@tbl-loadings)
- Phones lean towards **memory** or towards **cameras** (@fig-top-loadings)
:::
:::::
:::::::

::: notes
@tbl-loadings shows all loadings and @fig-top-loadings shows the three largest per component. Same colour means the specifications move together; opposite colours mean a trade-off. Processor speed also loads positively on PC2 (`r ld("PC2", "processor_speed")`). Before rotation, all variables tend to load highly on the first component, as the PCA lecture explains, which is why PC1 is an overall factor. Sign check for this render: PC1 all positive = `r pc1_all_positive`; PC2 storage positive and rear camera negative = `r pc2_storage_vs_camera`. If either is FALSE, the signs flipped on this computer: swap "high" and "low" in the wording on this slide and the next two.
:::

A phone is positioned with two levers: **how much hardware** it has (PC1) and **where that hardware goes** (PC2).

::::

::: notes
This is the descriptive analysis the brief asks for in part (a): the components are described with the six variables that built them. The `r nrow(pc_profile)` training phones are split into three equal groups by score with ntile(), and the original specifications are averaged in each group (@tbl-pc1-profile, @tbl-pc2-profile). The right-hand rows repeat the clearest low and high averages from the table. Blue = higher for high scorers; orange = lower for high scorers. These are descriptive averages, not significance tests. Click the second tab to show PC2.
:::

## Better-equipped phones cost more {.smaller}

::::::::: columns
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-price-map
#| fig-cap: "Price against overall performance score. Blue = leans towards memory and speed (PC2 above 0); orange = leans towards cameras (PC2 below 0). Lines show each group's trend."
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 5.6
phone_map |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = price, colour = focus)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = example_phones, size = 3.5, shape = 21,
             fill = "white", stroke = 1.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_label(data = example_phones,
             aes(x = PC1 + nudge_x, y = price * exp(nudge_y), label = label),
             colour = "#1F2933", fill = "white", size = 4.2,
             label.size = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(prefix = "RM "),
                breaks = c(200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = focus_colours) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 3))) +
  labs(x = "Overall performance score (PC1): low = budget, high = flagship",
       y = "Price (RM, log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_slides()
```
:::

[`r pc1_price_cor`]{.hero} [correlation between PC1 and log price]{.kicker}

[Redmi 12C RM `r ex_price("Redmi 12C")` to Galaxy S23 Ultra RM `r ex_price("Galaxy S23 Ultra")` (@fig-price-map)]{.note-line}

- **Blue above orange:** at the same score, memory-focused phones cost more (@fig-price-map)

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-tip title="So what"}
Price follows the **whole hardware bundle**, not camera megapixels alone.
:::
::::
:::::::
:::::::::

::: notes
This chart puts the two components into plain terms for a business audience. Each dot is one training phone. The x-axis is the PC1 score. Colour splits phones by the sign of their PC2 score: blue = above 0 (memory and speed), orange = below 0 (camera). Each line is a simple trend through one group, so the gap between the lines previews D's positive PC2 result. Price is on a log scale because it is right-skewed; equal steps up the axis are equal percentage increases. Prices were recorded in Indian rupees and are shown in ringgit at RM `r myr_per_100_inr` per 100 rupees (Bank Negara Malaysia, 6 October 2026, midpoint of buying and selling). Converting does not change the PCA or the regression results, only the axis labels. The iPhone 13 previews D's brand result. These are descriptive patterns; the regression controls for the other predictors.
:::

What drives smartphone prices

## Key findings {.smaller}

::::::: grid2
::: {.card .navy .fragment}
[1 · PCA]{.kicker} [Two components summarise the hardware]{.big}

Overall performance (PC1) and storage and speed vs camera (PC2) explain `r round(pc_cum, 1)`% of the six specifications (@fig-top-loadings)
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[2 · Specifications]{.kicker} [Better-equipped phones cost more]{.big}

Both components and screen size raise price at the 0.1% level; a larger battery lowers it (@tbl-specs)
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[3 · Connectivity]{.kicker} [NFC and 5G add a premium]{.big}

NFC at the 0.1% level and 5G at the 5% level, compared with phones without them (@tbl-specs)
:::

::: {.card .orange .fragment}
[4 · Brand]{.kicker} [Brand matters beyond hardware]{.big}

Apple, Samsung and Vivo are priced above Xiaomi, Motorola below; Oppo, Realme and Other do not differ (@tbl-brands)
:::
:::::::

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-important title="Bottom line"}
Price follows the **whole hardware bundle** and the **brand name**. At the same overall level, camera-focused phones are priced lower than memory-focused phones (@fig-price-map, @tbl-specs).
:::
::::

::: notes
Card 1 comes from the PCA (B and C). Cards 2 to 4 come from the regression (D) and were checked against the seed 41352 output: PC1, PC2, screen size, battery, NFC, Apple and Samsung at 0.1%; Vivo and Motorola at 1%; 5G at 5%; Oppo, Realme and Other not significant. "Raise price" means a positive significant influence on log price, holding the other variables constant. The bottom line follows from the positive PC2 coefficient. If the final numbers change, update this slide. @tbl-specs and @tbl-brands are D's tables, so these references only resolve in the merged slides.
:::
